KEY MESSAGE 1...Strong/long duration Nor'easter will continue to 
bring damaging wind gusts, coastal flooding/beach erosion, and 
periods of heavy rain through the weekend. Rain and gusty winds 
persist into  Monday. 

What's there to be said about the ongoing early season nor'easter 
that hasn't been said already...not much! Things are playing out 
largely as expected so far...OPC surface analysis indicates the 
996mb surface low spinning well to our south. It's on its way north, 
slowly, before it makes a sharp westward turn into New Jersey 
tonight/tomorrow. So far we've already seen some minor coastal 
flooding on Nantucket where ~2 feet of storm surge pushed water 
levels into minor flood stage during the overnight high tide. 
The area of most concern continues to be the east coast of MA, 
especially south of Boston, where a several factors are at play.
These include the long duration of the winds and long NE fetch,
inability for water to fully recede between high tides, and the
steadily rising astronomical tides. A Coastal Flood Warning 
remains in effect for these east facing locations where the 
greatest concern will be the Saturday afternoon and overnight 
high tides, though we'll be flirting with minor flooding 
through Sunday. A Coastal Flood Advisory is in effect for the 
south coast of Massachusetts and Rhode Island where more 
sporadic minor coastal flooding is possible due to high surf 
just offshore and increasing swells. 

Winds have increased as expected, with widespread gusts of 45 to 55 
mph observed from Cape Cod and the islands to coastal Rhode 
Island while several coastal stations have reported gusts 60+ 
mph. This occurred as the core of a 65kt LLJ moved overhead 
tonight and this continues to lift north and west (weakening) 
through Saturday and Sunday. That is why timing of the strongest
wind gusts won't be identical for everyone...more likely later 
Saturday into Sunday for northeast MA for example. Regardless, 
northeast winds will be relentlessly gusty through Sunday, 
gusting 35-45 mph for most inland locations and as high as 45-55
mph along the coast at times. The timing of this storm before 
trees have lost their leaves will exacerbate impacts from broken
limbs and increase the potential for power outages. Strong 
winds will continue through Sunday but won't be as strong as the
storm weakens. Even so, even Monday will be breezy and wet. 

This system will dump a lot of rain over the next 72 hours thanks to 
the impressive moisture and dynamics...anomalous PWATs and the 
previously mentioned 925mb jet along with orographic lift into the 
higher terrain. Rainfall totals of 3-5" are expected. The best 
chance at these higher amounts is along the coasts and the east 
slopes of the CT hills, Worcester hills. Flood risk will be 
mitigated by the long duration of the event, though pockets of urban 
and poor drainage flooding are possible.  

KEY MESSAGE 2...One final day of wet and unsettled weather Tuesday 
before a warming and drying trend arrives next week.

The first part of the extended forecast features lingering effects 
from our decaying nor'easter as the upper level low will be slow to 
exit. Thus, while we won't see the wind and rain that we saw over 
the weekend to start the work week, it will still be wet and 
unsettled. By Tuesday afternoon guidance shows gradual clearing from 
SW to NE with even some breaks of sunshine possible later in the 
afternoon! By Wednesday, the upper air pattern begins to change as a 
ridge builds over the eastern CONUS. By Thursday, 500mb heights 
build to 582dm and seems to persist through at least the end of the 
week across ensemble guidance. Closer to the surface, 850 mb 
temperature anomalies soar to +6-10C above climo through late week. 
At the surface this translates to a period of late-summer like 
warmth with highs in the upper 70s to perhaps low 80s inland. 
Outside of Tuesday, the only chance for any  precipitation arrives 
later Thursday into Friday as a weakening shortwave approaches the 
region from the west.
